The main river works for the substructure of sustainable transport bridge are now complete, and the remaining river 
works to build temporary support piers and pier protection systems will be completed for the arrival of the bridge 
superstructure from Belgium next Spring. In the meantime, the fi t-out of the bridge superstructure with the automated 
mechanical and electrical plant needed for the opening of the central bridge spans is progressing in Belgium. The 
construction of the new public plaza area on the south quays is ongoing and foundation slabs are complete.
The reinforced concrete frame of the main Transport Hub building is complete and internal blockwork etc. is ongoing 
within the building. The main structural steelwork for the roof of the Transport Hub is nearing completion and the 
installation of the roof decking is progressing. The foundations for the western pedestrian footbridge over the railway 
line have commenced.   
The new permanent traffi c lights at the junction of Abbey Road and Fountain Street are now in operation, but traffi c 
management continues in operation for pedestrians to facilitate ongoing footpath works. The inbound footpath and 
adjacent traffi c lane on Fountain Street are also currently closed to facilitate these works, which will continue into 
December. Accommodation works and roadworks also continue on Abbey Road with traffi c management in place to 
facilitate the new access arrangements for the schools and other properties. Single lane traffi c management continues 
in operation along Dock Road to facilitate adjacent bridge works and central median works. The roadworks in Ferrybank 
will continue in the run up to Christmas and the Winterval Festival, and traffi c will continue to be managed and 
monitored during this period. Arrangements to start construction works for the railway fl ood defence and drainage works 
are currently being fi nalised. These works are designed 
to make the existing and new rail infrastructure climate 
resilient into the future and protect it from the increasing 
impacts of climate change. The works will include the 
construction of a trackside steel pile fl ood wall, drainage 
network and pumping stations from the Sally Park side, 
through Plunkett Station car parks and through the full 
extent of the North Quays site and will involve deep pile 
driving and excavations beside the live commuter and 
freight railway lines. The project is liaising with Irish Rail 
in the management of the construction works to 
maximise effi ciency and minimise impacts on rail lines 
and services.

Outdoor Recreation Infrastructure Scheme (ORIS) 2024/2025
The Minister for Rural and Community Development, Heather Humphreys TD, launched the 2024/2025 Outdoor 
Recreation Infrastructure Scheme on 17th October last. WCCC will administer the scheme and on 25th October issued 
a call for Expressions of Interest to community groups and Trail Management Organisations in Waterford.
Expression of interest forms and scheme guidelines can be downloaded here or obtained by e-mailing 
outdoorrecreation@waterfordcouncil.ie. All those submitting an expression of interest form should, in the first instance 
make themselves aware of the scheme guidelines particularly regarding their proposal’s eligibility.
Completed expression of interest forms must be emailed to outdoorrecreation@waterfordcouncil.ie before 5.00pm 
Friday 22nd November 2024. Expressions of interest received after this date and time will not be considered for the 
2024/2025 scheme. All applications will be subject to a selection process using national criteria. Selected expression of 
interest applications will be developed into detailed bids for consideration for ORIS 2024/2025.
County Outdoor Recreation Plan
Work has commenced on the preparation of the County Outdoor Recreation Plan (CORP) for Waterford. It is an objec-
tive of ‘Embracing Ireland’s Outdoors – The National Outdoor Recreation Strategy’ that each county prepares a CORP 
and forms a stakeholder grouping the County Outdoor Recreation Committee. In this regard progress to date has been:
•	
Outscape has been appointed to assist in the preparation of the plan over the coming months.
•	
Stakeholder and public consultation will form a key part of the preparation of the plan in the coming weeks.
•	
It is anticipated that the CORP will be finalized by late Q1/early Q2 2025

Development Plan and Strategic Environmental Assessment (SEA) Monitoring
Section 15 of the PDA 2000 places a general duty on a planning authority to take such steps within its power, as may 
be necessary, to secure the objectives of its development plan. Not more than two years after the making of the de-
velopment plan, the Chief Executive is required to give a report to the members of the planning authority on progress 
achieved in securing objectives of the plan. 
Circulated for the November Plenary Council meeting are two important reports which:
1.Monitor the implementation of the development plan, consistent with Section 15(2) of the Planning and Development 
Act 2000, as amended. The Section 15 Report will also be furnished to the Offi ce of the Planning Regulator as part of 
the annual development plan monitoring required pursuant to Chapter 10 of the Development Plans: Guidelines for 
Planning Authorities (DHLGH) 2022 and as set out in Appendix 16 of the development plan.
2.Monitor the impact on the environment of the development plan implementation, consistent with Article 13J of the 
Planning and Development (Strategic Environmental Assessment) Regulations 2004. This has been prepared iteratively 
and in tandem with the Section 15 report by ARUP on behalf of WCCC. 
The reports are important documents which will inform further discussion with both the Planning SPC and the Plenary 
Council on any changes required to support full implementation of the plan. 
Residential Zoned Land Tax (RZLT) Draft Annual Revised Map
On the 1st day of February last, Waterford City and County Council prepared and published the RZLT draft annual 
revised map for the 2025 tax liability yea. The following stages and timeline apply to the annual mapping process:
1.Publication of a draft annual revised map followed by a 2-month period of public consultation, accompanied by place-
ment of advertisements in local press and across Waterford Council social media accounts;
2.Receipt of written submissions from landowners and consideration thereof;
3.Notifi cation of written determinations made by Waterford Council to the relevant landowners who made written sub-
missions to the draft map;

Heritage Officer Report 
The Waterford City and County Heritage Forum has prepared a Draft Heritage Strategy 2025-2030 and is inviting input 
from the public.  The Strategy can be viewed on https://consult.waterfordcouncil.ie/en/consultation/draft-waterford-heri-
tage-strategy-2025-2030. The Heritage Strategy sets out strategic objectives relevant to all aspects of heritage including 
archaeology, built, cultural, intangible and natural heritage which will guide annual action plans to achieve those 
objectives. 
The public are invited to make a   submission on the Draft Strategy   by Friday 8th November 2024 to Bernadette Guest, 
Heritage Officer, Waterford City and County Council, Menapia Building, The Mall, Waterford  
bguest@waterfordcouncil.ie
Decade of Commemorations
A Screening of The Aftermath, a film by John Foley and funded by Waterford City and Council Commemorations 
Committee will take place in Dungarvan Cinema on Wednesday, November 13th at 8pm in Garter Lane Theatre. The 
Aftermath captures the memories and thoughts of Waterford people talking about their ancestors involved in the War 
of Independence and the Civil War. The documentary film looks at some of the key events and the people involved 
and also looks at what happened to those involved in the decades following the period. The film was funded through 
the Department of Tourism, Culture, Arts, Gaeltact, Sports and Media’s Decade of Commemorations Fund.   See www.
facebook.com/johnfoleyimages for details of further screenings.
ACTIVE LAND MANAGEMENT AND DERELICT SITES TEAM
The team is currently addressing a total of 299 properties classified as either derelict or potentially derelict. Recent 
weeks and months have seen a significant increase in activity, with 96 properties now listed on the Derelict Sites 
Register. Initial engagement with property owners or their representatives is crucial for resolving issues related to 
dereliction and for gaining insights into the various factors contributing to the properties’ current state. 
4.Making of appeals to An Bord Pleanála where landowners are aggrieved by the determination of the council; and,
5.Publication of final annual revised map at the start of the relevant tax liability year followed by a repeat of the process 
to prepare a new draft annual revised map. 
We are currently in stage 5 in this timeline. A total of two appeals (ref WFD - C30 - 10 and WFD - C30 - 14) have been 
made to An Bord Pleanála relating to our own determinations to retain lands as in-scope for the purposes of the tax. The 
final determinations of An Bord Pleanála have upheld the view of the planning authority, and the relevant lands remain 
in-scope for the tax.  We will now proceed to publish the final annual map for 31st January 2025 and prepare a new draft 
annual revised map for publication on the 1st February 2025.

•Connecting Community Roadshows: Preparations are in progress for 2025 roadshows, which aim to bring public services 
directly to communities. We are delighted to have been nominated for a National Chambers Local Government Excellence 
Award. The awards ceremony will take place on November 25th. The 2025 roadshows will expand to include new areas, 
with a core objective of providing accessible public services to the public. Each event will feature over 25 exhibitors, offer-
ing valuable resources and information to meet community needs.
•Community Playful Streets 2024:  A review is scheduled for November 14th, bringing together multiple agencies to plan 
the 2025 programME. Building on the success of 2024, these projects will be integrated into various strategic initiatives, in-
cluding the Climate Action Plan and Waterford CYPSY. The 2025 plans aim to expand on this year’s achievements, which 
saw over 2,500 participants across 34 communities and events. The goal is to continue to foster community engagement 
and well-being through play-focused activities, while supporting broader environmental and social objectives.
•Community Wellbeing Seminars: A successful pilot event was held on November 23rd. Building on this success, two 
additional seminars are planned on November 21st and another during the week of December 2nd. If participation and 
feedback remain positive, the programME will be expanded to include a series of seminars throughout 2025, aiming to 
reach a wider audience and promote community health and well-being.
•Place Standard: This framework helps communities assess and improve the quality of their local areas. It focuses on both 
the physical environment and the social aspects.

featured speakers from the Department of Rural and Community Development (DRCD), Social Enterprise Republic of 
Ireland (SERI), and Connected Hubs, as well as local representatives from Waterford City and County Council (WCCC), 
Waterford Leader, and Waterford Area Partnership. The speakers provided valuable insights into the potential and growth 
opportunities for community social enterprises. As a direct outcome, a fully funded research student from SETU has been 
appointed to begin research in this area. All event materials are available upon request and will be distributed to attendees 
shortly.
•WHO Healthy City Accreditation: Work is underway to have Waterford City accredited to the WHO Healthy Cities 
programME. Waterford currently holds a representative position on the National Network. Political leadership will be 
sought to further enhance the bid in Q4 of 2024.

working groups, ensuring WCCC is represented and contributing to the Wellbeing agenda within the city and county.

Health and Pobal, while also providing tailored advice and guidance on health and well-being interventions across 
communities.

ENVIRONMENTAL EDUCATION & AWARENESS
Schools Programmes
The Tom Murphy Litter Competition for Secondary Schools has begun for 2024. All participating schools received clean 
up materials to take part, including litter pickers, high visibility vests, gloves and bags. Schools are now busy carrying 
out regular clean ups between now and the end of December, with some schools carrying out over 3 clean ups a week 
with different classes. Judging will  take place during December. Tom Murphy Car Sales have sponsored the prize find of 
€1500 for the winning school. The prizegiving and presentation of certificates of participation will take place in the Mayors 
Parlour in January. 
Green Schools visits are underway, with some schools requesting advice and help with their work while others are availing 
of an early assessment visit to their school. The teacher seminars took place online in October last month to ensure that 
teachers knew what to expect in the coming year for their current Green Schools theme. 
We are running a full day’s workshop for Green School Committees in Waterford primary schools to teach students and 
teachers alike about the circular economy. This will introduce the idea of the circular economy to pupils and encourage 
them to think about how to design items with that in mind. For teachers, they will go away with knowledge needed to run 
similar workshops/ classes in their school. 
35 Waterford primary schools are participating in the Picker Pals litter programme once again this school year. This pro-
gramme is most suitable for 1st and 2nd class children but has classes participating from 3rd, 4th and 5th class also. It 
teaches about litter and involves activity based learning to promote a keen sense of responsibility for the environment. 
The 8 Secondary Schools taking part in the Composting for Schools programme have received their initial visit. The main 
purpose of this visit was to carry out a waste audit to help schools to prevent, reduce and reuse their waste, with a strong 
focus on recycling food waste. Schools have also taken part in 5 online sessions to learn more about waste prevention, 
recycling and composting within a school.

Circular Living Month 
Globally more textiles are consumed than ever before and Ireland is no exception. An EPA study carried out by 
researchers at MTU in 2019 found that the per capita consumption of new textiles in Ireland is 53 kg per person per year 
– that’s almost 1 kg/week of new textiles purchased by every citizen. During October there was a national focus on the 
circular economy for Circular Living month, with an emphasis on repair and reuse. We ran a series of 4 weekly workshops 
to teach participants sewing repair for clothes. There was also a sewing repair demonstration and a clothes swap and 
bike repair event. 
CLIMATE ACTION
Business Pledge for a Cleaner Greener Waterford
Over 1,000 businesses made the pledge to create a greener 
Waterford before the October 18th deadline. These businesses have 
set out what they would like to do in the next year to become more 
sustainable. From hotels to mechanics and onto manufacturing, 
these businesses will get support over the next few from the Climate 
Team to make the actions they have set out a reality. Saving the 
businesses money and helping them to avail of grants and pitch their 
sustainability credentials to win business
Reusing and Repairing in October
October is national reuse month and many members of the public 
took advantage of the opportunity to improve their sewing skills and 
reduce the amount of waste we send to landfi ll. There were sewing 
classes and clothes swaps. Around the world the equivalent of one 
rubbish truck of clothes per second is disposed of, learning how to 
repair and keeping our clothes in circulation for much longer reduces 
that fi gure.
Going back to school on air quality
Four schools are currently participating in air quality monitoring 
programmes. 2 Primary Schools  start monitoring the air quality in 
their area next week after designing a banner for their school and 
participating in workshops on how we can reduce air pollution. 
2 Secondary Schools are also monitoring air quality. In partnership 
with local technology company trilateral they have mapped the air 
quality around their school and will work with their classmates to re-
duce particulates.
